task: Write one sentence of your own using the word vernacular. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know vernacular should be able to work it out from your sentence.

Verna — the household-born slave of a Roman family — gave English exactly one word and stopped. Its look-alike vernal belongs to a different root entirely, ver ('spring'), so the family tree here has a single branch: the home-born tongue, the vernacular.
Vernacular means the everyday language actually spoken by the people of a place or group, as opposed to formal, literary, or official language.

For centuries, European scholars wrote serious books only in Latin; when Dante chose to write his epic in the vernacular — the Italian his neighbors actually spoke at the market — he was gambling that everyday speech could carry great literature.
The gamble made the poem immortal.
The vernacular is the language people live in: the words of the market, the kitchen, and the street rather than the courtroom or the scholarly page.
Dante's choice looks obvious now precisely because the everyday tongue won — and the word still marks that split between official language and the speech of ordinary life.
Vernacular draws one line: the language people actually live in versus the official, literary, or technical registers above it.

Keep its neighbors straight — a dialect is a region's own variety, grammar and accent included; slang is the casual, fast-changing edge of in-group talk; and when a profession's insider terms shut ordinary listeners out, that is jargon, not vernacular.
The vernacular is precisely what the shut-out listener speaks.
(As an adjective, vernacular architecture means local, homegrown building styles — the same idea in bricks.)

The poetry prize went, controversially, to a collection written the way Ana's neighborhood actually talks.
Ana had drafted the poems twice -- first in the polished literary English her professors rewarded, then again in the vernacular of her block: bus-stop talk, kitchen talk, corner-store talk.
One judge objected that the second version was not 'literary language' at all.
Another answered that this was precisely the achievement.
The poems' grammar follows the block's own rules, consistent as any textbook's, and readers from the neighborhood recite whole pages from memory.
Ana shrugs at the argument.
'I wrote it in the language my readers already live in,' she says.
